PUTTEE (Winnipeg) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 95) to amend the Conciliation Act, 1900. He said : This Bill is exactly similar to the one that was presented by myself last year, and I presume that during that time it has received some consideration at the hands of the Minister of Labour. In dealing with this matter I might express the wish that the Minister of Labour would give us his own opin-

ion, and some account of the actual operations of the Conciliation Act during the three years it has been in force. There are at the present time, as was shown by the debate in this House last week, a large number of industrial disturbances in the Dominion, In nearly every province attention is being drawn to disagreements between capital and labour; therefore I think, Mr. Speaker, the House will be inclined to give some attention to a proposition which aims to improve the Conciliation Act as much as possible. I notice that the Minister of I,a hour has gone definitely upon record as altogether in favour of the principle of compulsory investigation rather than compulsory arbitration. I would like to be able to think that these attempts and these experiments that he is making would be effective. But I cannot persuade myself that they will be really effective, not that they will not affect any disputes, but that they will not practically affect any considerable number of the disputes that we are having and that we are likely to have in the future. I submit that we have no warrant whatever to expect in the near future any cessation in the number of labour disputes in this country.
We have seen during the last five years, and more than ever during the last three years, an increase in the number of these disputes. The reason probably has been the general wave of prosperity that has advanced over the country. Everything has been advancing in price, in cost, and labour seems always to be the last to advance and to obtain a share of the prosperity. In this respect prosperity has been practically a curse to the wage earner. The wage earner, whose wages have a tendency to remain at the same figure, cannot get them advanced in many instances without going in to industrial trouble, and he has often had to sacrifice weeks and weeks of his salary in an attempt to get his wage scaled up to meet the requirements called for by the increased cost of everything on which he has to spend his wages.	Speaking especially for the
city I know best, prosperity has been a most serious drawback to the men who work for wages. Of course, I claim that we have no right, at all events, to condemn the principle of compulsory arbitration so far as we know what its record has been. It has only been in operation seven or eight years, I think, under a British form of government, t^t, is in New Zealand. They have experience there as well as we have in rising, markets, and there is no doubt that the Act has been successful in abolishing strikes. There is some difference of opinion at whose cost success has been gained. It is very generally supposed that the worker has gained the largest number of awards made. On the other hand, I think we can find in New Zealand itself that the workers, although they agree to the prin- j

ciple are no more enthusiastically in favour of it than are the employers themselves. The employers claim this one thing for the Act, at all events, that it has abolished suicidal and industrial disputes in the matter of strikes and lockouts.
It is taken into the court; it is separate altogether from the local court, but, at the same time into the court where the dispute is considered and adjusted while the men are at work, while the wages are being paid, while industry is continued, and whatever the result is you have the award loyally accepted by both sides. At the present time I believe there is a probability of one award finally being put to test. For myself, I shall watch with some concern the outcome of this matter, although I am not prepared at all to agree in advance that any objection to an award, either on the part of an employer, if the award may be against him, or on the part of the employee, if the award be against him, or if one or two objections are to be taken, it shall be considered as a condemnation of the principle of compulsory arbitration. If it were possible, and I believe most things are possible in this country, if we attempt them in the right way, even by means of legislation in this House, I favouy this principle because I believe it makes for industrial peace. In view of the enormous distance that there is in this countrv between the present condition and industrial peace, I believe it is something to be looked for and to be worked for. The Bill that I have introduced simply attempts, or seeks to amend the Conciliation Act of 1900. I am ready to believe that there is some merit in the suggestions that have been put into these clauses because I find the tdea exactly carried out in the Bill that this House was discussing the other evening, called an Act to aid in the settlement of railway labour disputes. That Bill seeks practically to apply the same principle that is involved in Bill No. 95, but it applies it only to railways. There seems to be no doubt that the promoter of the Bill expects good to result from it, but the question that is raised and the question that must be raised in everybody's mind is: Why not extend the principle of that Bill to other industries that we can affect, to the mines especially and to large manufacturing industries ? I believe, Mr. Speaker, that if the principle is good in connection with railways, it would be equally good in connection with the general industries of the country, and I do submit that the probabilities are that it would be a great deal more useful and that it would certainly be a good deal more availed of. At the present time, as was shown in the debate the other evening, the larger organizations in connection with railways have got beyond that period in the life of labour organizations when strikes are necessary. They no longer strike. The principal railway organ!-

zations of this country and of this continent no longer have to resort to strikes. Their differences are settled by conciliation, by conferences, by appeals, first to one official then to another official, right up to tile vicepresidents and presidents of the road, and if there is no agreement then come to with the representatives of the railway system, the chief officers of other systems are called in both by the railway corporations and by the labour organizations. This practice for the last eight or ten years, has resulted in practically abolishing strikes on Canadian railways in so far as the old established brotherhoods are concerned. Strikes by the newer organizations which are brought about by the desire of the railway companies not to have to deal with any other bodies of employees as bodies, are continually arising, they will arise in future and this railway Conciliation Bill will be brought into operation to that extent, but I believe not in the same degree as it would be if applied to the general business of the country. Although the Conciliation Act is something to the credit of the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock), I believe he could tell us that it does not, as a matter of fact, affect many of the disputes that arise, and that under this Act they are settled neither satisfactorily nor unsatisfactorily, because they simply wear themselves out in the course of time, and the reason for this is not because the parties to the dispute are necessarily opposed to conciliation. In any serious dispute, I take it, and it is a fact, that either party would welcome conciliation if it could be brought about by a third party without either of the disputants appearing to solicit it, because, in the matter of a labour dispute, as in a larger dispute, the party who is calling for an armistice, the party who is calling for cessation of hostilities or for intervention, is practically admitting that he is beaten, and employers will not ask for conciliation because they are afraid it will give heart to the men on strike, and labour organizations which have a strong fund to support their members, are reluctant to ask for conciliation because they are afraid it will be taken as an admission that they have lost the day, and that finally in the award it will be used against them. It was this important consideration, I believe, in connection with the big strike in New Zealand, in 1890 or 1892, that first led the statesmen of that country to formulate their Compulsory Arbitration Act, which Act practically operates altogether independently of the expressed wish of either of the parties. I believe that if our Conciliation Act could be so amended that it could be put into operation, at all events, as far as conciliation is concerned, and if the minister had the power and also the duty in connection with the labour dispute of making an investigation and attempting conciliation, the probability is that it would be found easy to bring the
parties together and would result in the ending of many industrial disputes.
I understand my hon. friend (Mr. Puttee) has not concluded his remarks ?
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: No, I have not quite concluded.

Mr. Speaker, out of respect to the memory of the late Mr. Justice Mills, for a long time a prominent and very much respected member of this House, and so as to permit hon. members to attend his funeral, which will take place this evening, I now have the honour to move that the House do adjourn.

I esteem it my duty, Sir, under the circumstances and out of the respect that we owe to the gentleman who was so long a prominent figure in the public life of Canada, and who at the time of his death occupied a very high position on a judicial bench, of this country, to second the motion.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 6 o'clock.
Tuesday, May 12, 1903.
